## Part 1 · 00:04

[00:04] I'm Bart Ehrman and I'm happy to announce that I'm going to be doing another course on another book of the Bible. This time it's the Gospel of Luke. I'm particularly happy to be doing this course because in my first semester of my first year in graduate school, Luke was the first Bible book that I had a course on. I've been studying this thing since 1978. I'm calling the course Luke's Maverick Gospel, a vision of reverses. It'll be an eight-lecture course spread out over two days, a Saturday and Sunday with a Q&A at the end of each day. And so, this will be May 10th and May 11th.

[00:48] Many readers of the New Testament don't fully appreciate how different the Gospel of Luke is from the other three Gospels. It's often simply considered to deliver the same basic message as Matthew and Mark with a few extra stories thrown in, such as the parables of the Good Samaritan the Prodigal Son and the Rich Man and Lazarus. But in this view, basically, it conveys the same message. A closer look shows that that's not true at all. Certainly, Luke contains much the same outline as Mark and especially Matthew.

[01:30] For example, with tales of Jesus' birth, baptism, miracles, teaching, death, and resurrection. But what it actually says about these events is in many ways very different. This becomes clear when you ask pointed questions about key issues in the Gospels. Did Jesus become the Son of God at his baptism? Did Jesus plan to take his message to non-Jews? Did Jesus expect the end to come in the lifetime of his disciples? Was Jesus distraught at the end, wondering why God had forsaken him? Did Jesus' death bring an atonement for the sins of others?

[02:13] The answers depend on whether you're reading Luke or one of the other Synoptic Gospels. In this course, we'll be exploring Luke's distinctive portrayal of Jesus, asking these and many other key questions. Among other things, we'll see how in many ways, and surprisingly, even to many scholars, even though Luke was probably the last of the Synoptic Gospels to be written, it appears that in some important respects, including the question of how a person can be made right with God, it represents Jesus' own views better than Matthew and Mark do.

[02:50] And so again, I'm calling it Luke's Maverick Gospel, a vision of reversals. It'll be an eight-lecture over two days with two Q&A's on May 10th and 11th. For more information and registration, go to bartdherman.com/learnluke. I hope to see you there.
